meta.titre: Synovial Joints in Action: Friction, Lubrication and Antagonistic Muscles at the Elbow
meta.sous_theme: Parts of a synovial joint, types of joint and the muscles that move the elbow

sections.contenu_markdown:
A girl lifts a bucket of water from the ground to her chest at a stand-pipe in her village.
Her elbow bends smoothly, over and over, without any grinding between the bones.
GCE Biology asks which structure lowers friction, which joint allows which movement and which muscle straightens the arm.
This course explains the working of a synovial joint so that each of these answers follows from the structure.

items: The humerus is the bone of the upper arm; the radius and ulna are the bones of the forearm.
A joint is a place where two or more bones meet.
Muscles can only pull when they contract; they cannot push.

sections.titre: How a synovial joint is built and works
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Synovial joints
Joints in the skull are fixed and those between the vertebrae move only a little. **Synovial joints** are freely movable. The elbow, knee, shoulder and hip are examples.

### Parts of a synovial joint

| Part | What it is | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Articular cartilage | Smooth layer on the ends of the bones | Reduces friction and absorbs shock |
| Synovial membrane | Lining of the joint capsule | Makes synovial fluid |
| Synovial fluid | Slippery liquid in the joint cavity | Lubricates the joint, reduces friction and supplies nutrients to cartilage |
| Joint capsule | Tough covering around the joint | Holds the bones together and keeps in the fluid |
| Ligaments | Strong fibres joining bone to bone | Hold bones in place and prevent dislocation |

Tendons are different from ligaments: **tendons join muscle to bone**.

### Types of synovial joint

| Type | Examples | Movement |
|---|---|---|
| Hinge | Elbow, knee | Back and forth in one plane only |
| Ball-and-socket | Shoulder, hip | Movement in many directions, including rotation |
| Pivot | Between the first two neck bones | Turning the head from side to side |

### Antagonistic muscles at the elbow
Muscles work in pairs. To **bend** (flex) the arm, the biceps contracts and the triceps relaxes. To **straighten** (extend) the arm, the triceps contracts and the biceps relaxes. The biceps is joined by a tendon to the radius; the triceps is joined by a tendon to the ulna.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks about friction or lubrication in a joint
variantes.contenu_markdown: Synovial fluid is the lubricant. Cartilage gives a smooth surface. If both appear, choose the one that matches the wording: 'lubricates' means synovial fluid and 'smooth covering' means cartilage.

variantes.nom: Naming a joint from the movement
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a description of movement is given
variantes.contenu_markdown: One plane only means a hinge joint. Movement all round means ball-and-socket. Turning on an axis, as in turning the head from side to side, means a pivot joint.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a movement of the forearm is described
variantes.contenu_markdown: Say which muscle contracts and which relaxes. For extension of the forearm the answer is the triceps.

sections.enonce_markdown:
A girl bends her arm to lift a bucket of water to her chest.

(a) Name the type of joint at her elbow.

(b) Which muscle contracts and which relaxes?

(c) What joins the contracting muscle to the bone?

(d) Name the structure that stops the bones of the elbow from rubbing together.

etapes.justification: The arm bends back and forth in one plane.
One plane of movement means a hinge.
To bend the arm the biceps shortens while the triceps lengthens.
Muscle is joined to bone by a tendon, not a ligament.
Cartilage covers the bone ends and synovial fluid lubricates.

sections.conclusion_markdown: (a) **Hinge joint.** (b) **The biceps contracts and the triceps relaxes.** (c) **A tendon.** (d) **Articular cartilage, with synovial fluid as lubricant.**

items.pourquoi_faux: Ligaments join bone to bone; tendons join muscle to bone.
items.correction_markdown: Tendon: muscle to bone. Ligament: bone to bone.

items.erreur_markdown: The triceps pushes the forearm straight.
items.pourquoi_faux: Muscles can only pull. The triceps pulls the ulna when it contracts.
items.correction_markdown: The triceps contracts and pulls, while the biceps relaxes.

items.erreur_markdown: The elbow is a ball-and-socket joint.
items.pourquoi_faux: The elbow bends in one plane only, which is the movement of a hinge. The shoulder and hip are ball-and-socket joints.
items.correction_markdown: Elbow and knee: hinge. Shoulder and hip: ball-and-socket.

items.erreur_markdown: Synovial fluid is produced by the cartilage.
items.pourquoi_faux: The synovial membrane produces the fluid.

items.erreur_markdown: To bend the arm, the biceps and triceps both contract.
items.pourquoi_faux: If both contracted, they would pull against each other and the arm would not move.
items.correction_markdown: One muscle contracts and its partner relaxes.

items.enonce_markdown: Match each part to its function: (i) ligament, (ii) articular cartilage, (iii) synovial fluid. Functions: A: lubricates the joint; B: holds bone to bone; C: gives a smooth surface that absorbs shock.

(a) Name the type of joint at the hip and the type at the knee.

(b) Explain why the hip can move in more directions than the knee.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Hip: **ball-and-socket joint**. Knee: **hinge joint**.

(b) In a ball-and-socket joint the rounded end of one bone fits into a cup-shaped socket, so it can swing and rotate in many directions. A hinge joint allows movement in one plane only.

items.enonce_markdown:
A student straightens her arm from a bent position and then bends it again.

(a) Name the muscle that contracts in each movement.

(b) Explain why two muscles are needed for these movements.

(c) Predict one effect on the joint if the synovial membrane were damaged and stopped producing fluid.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Straightening: the **triceps** contracts. Bending: the **biceps** contracts.

(b) A muscle can only pull when it contracts, so it cannot lengthen itself again. One muscle pulls the bone one way and its partner pulls it back (antagonistic pair).

(c) With less lubrication, friction between the cartilage surfaces would be greater, so the joint would move less smoothly and the cartilage would wear and receive fewer nutrients.

items_markdown: A synovial joint is freely movable; its parts are cartilage, synovial membrane, synovial fluid, capsule and ligaments.
Synovial fluid lubricates and cartilage gives a smooth shock-absorbing surface; both reduce friction.
Ligaments join bone to bone; tendons join muscle to bone.
Hinge joints (elbow, knee) move in one plane; ball-and-socket joints (shoulder, hip) move in many directions.
Muscles work in antagonistic pairs: biceps bends the arm and triceps straightens it, one contracting while the other relaxes.
